layout_dets.text: CORROSION BEHAVIOUR OF MOLYBDENUM-IMPLANTED

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: STAINLESS STEEL

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: M.B. IVES, U. G. AKANO1, Y.C. LU, GUO RUIJIN², S.C. SRIVASTAVA³

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Institute for Materials Research, McMaster University

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ABSTRACT

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A low-molybdenum austenitic stainless steel (UNS S30100) has been surface implanted with molybdenum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ions, using various doses of 50 keV and 140 keV ions at room temperature. It is found that in aqueous

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sulphate/chloride solutions similar to the constitution of sea-waters the implantation does not affect the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potentiostatically-determined critical pitting potential, but does change the density and morphology of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corrosion pits. Pitting initiation after the addition of chloride at a fixed potential indicates little change in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the time for measurable current increase, but the rate of increase of the current is much lower for implanted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: material. Detailed examination using optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, transmission electron

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: microscopy and selected area diffraction suggests that the pits produced in implanted material are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hemispherical with smooth covers of unattacked alloy. The use of half-implanted samples demonstrates that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: molybdenum implantation causes the formation of smooth-covered pits rather than "lacy" attack characteristic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of stainless steel attack in chloride solutions. The energy of implantation also affects the density of pit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nucleation, suggesting that passive films formed after implantation at low energies are not able to completely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: protect the steel surfaces.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: KEYWORDS

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: austenitic stainless steel; molybdenum; ion implantation; pitting corrosion; Rutherford backscatter

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spectroscopy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: INTRODUCTION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It is known that the addition of molybdenum to austenitic stainless steels increases their pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corrosion resistance in chloride-containing aqueous environments. This is demonstrated, for example,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by a shift of the critical pitting potential towards a more noble value (1),(2),(3) and by the incrcase in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the critical pitting temperature with increasing molybdenum alloy content (4),(5). It is known that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: molybdenum incorporates itself into the protective passive film (6),(7), and some have reported that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: presence of molybdenum in these alloys appears to promote a generally thicker passive film, with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: thickness tending to be proportional to the molybdenum content of the alloy (8). But how this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: improves the resistance to chloride attack remains unclear, although models describing competitive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: adsorption have becn proposed.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Ashworth et al. (9),(10),(11) have studied the properties of molybdenum-implanted Type UNS S30400

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stainless steel, finding that such a treated alloy behaved like the higher-molybdenum steel, type UNS

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: S31600, at least as far as pitting resistance is concerned. It was found that after three successive

layout_dets.text: polarization sweeps, some 36% of the implanted dose had been removed from the surface. However,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it was not possible to determine in what manner the molybdenum had been dissolved, or the precise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mechanism through which it improves the pitting resistance of the alloy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The present study was made in order to elucidate the mechanism by which molybdenum controls pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: susceptibility, by implanting known quantities of molybdenum ions into the near-surface region of a low-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: molybdenum stainless steel.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A 2 mm thick sheet of annealed UNS S30100 austenitic stainless steel was the starting material for this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: study. The chemical analysis of this alloy is shown in Table 1.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Table 1: Composition of the Alloy Used (in weight %)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Samples were cut into 10 mm circular discs, designed either to fit into a specially constructed Teflon

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sample holder or to be coated at the edges and back with a protective epoxy (Lepage "5-minute"), for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the electrochemical measurements. One side of each disc was metallographically polished to 1 micron

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diamond finish before ion implantation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The steel samples were ion-implanted at room temperature, using the McMaster 400 keV ion implanter,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: described elsewhere (12) equipped with a universal ion source capable of producing sharply focused

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gaseous and solid ion beams. The ion beam was rastered across the sample using a pair of electrostatic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: beam sweep plates, so that the beam covered an area of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at a current density of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The molybdenum source used consisted of a heated molybdenum wire over which oxygen gas is passed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to improve ionization. Two implantation energies, viz. 50 keV and 140 keV, were used in this work.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Rutherford backscattering spectroscopy (RBS) was used to analyze the implanted samples for the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: retained molybdenum dose and distribution, either before or after anodic dissolution. Each

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: backscattering spectrum was obtained, at a scattering angle of 160°, using 4 x

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: C of 2.0 MeV helium

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ions produced in a Van der Graaf accelerator.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 1 is a typical RBS spectrum of a molybdenum-implanted stainless steel specimen. It shows the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: contributions from the host metal (iron) atoms and the implanted molybdenum peak centred at channel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 382. From this spectrum it may be determined that the maximum molybdenum concentration is beneath

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the alloy surface, denoted by the arrows, as would be expected from the physics of the implantation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: process. By integrating the area under the molybdenum peak, the total retained dose can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: determined. The concentration of implanted ions, as a function of distance into the alloy surface, can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be obtained from the RBS spectrum, by taking into account the sputter erosion of the surface by the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implantation beam. The best fit to the data was obtained by assuming a sputter efficiency of 2.3

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: atoms/ion. Figure 2 shows such a relationship for two samples implanted with approximately the same

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dose, but at different implantation energies. It is seen that implanting at 140 keV produces a deeper

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and more uniform implant distribution.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Table 2 summarizes the data obtained on all the samples studied in this work, including the measured

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: retained dose and the surface and maximum molybdenum concentrations. The implantation clearly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: produces local molybdenum concentrations far in excess of those normally present in molybdenum-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: containing commercial stainless steels. However, these high concentrations are localized, since the peaks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in concentration are typically between 10 and 20 nm, and significant concentrations are rarely deeper

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than 40 nm, as seen in Fig. 2.

layout_dets.text: Microstructural Examination

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A combination of optical and electron-optical microscopy revealed both the extent of local attack on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the implanted samples and the detailed form of the particular pits produced in samples with high doses

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of implanted molybdenum. The low-dose samples (#1 and #2) showed no difference in pitting attack

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: morphology to the unimplanted control samples.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A comparison of the pitting characteristics of the implanted and unimplanted material was demonstrated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particularly vividly on a sample which had been ion-implanted over only half its surface area, by masking

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the sample in the implanter. Figure 5(a) shows an optical micrograph of this sample, after anodic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: polarization at 600 mV(SCE) for a time necessary to pass 1 C/cm² of total charge through the sample.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The differences in attack of the unimplanted and implanted regions of the surface, and the straight

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: boundary between them, are clearly seen. In particular, the unimplanted alloy exhibits relatively large

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: irregular pits, exhibiting a "lacy" surround, as originally reported some years ago by Rosenfeld and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Danilov (13), and typical of pits produced in this alloy under potentiostatic control, as shown in more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: detail in Fig. 5(b). In contrast, the implanted region shows a much higher density of smaller pits which,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on examination at higher resolution with scanning electron microscopy, are seen (Fig. 6(a).) to be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: completely circular in outline and covered by smooth caps. In addition, a few pits were found to have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: formed along the boundary between the implanted and unimplanted region and exhibited features

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: appropriate to both regions, as shown in Fig. 6(b).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A number of aspects of these pit fcatures were examined in greater detail. High-resolution Auger

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: electron spectroscopy (AES) was not particularly helpful in determining the nature of the covers. A

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cover was extracted for examination by floating it onto an aluminum grid and placing in a Philips EM-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 301 electron microscope. Figure 7(a) shows the bright field transmission image of the pieces of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: broken cover. Energy dispersive X-ray analysis showed high concentrations of the component metal ions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the alloy, suggesting that the cover comprises a significant amount of alloy metal. This conclusion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was confirmed by examination of the selected area diffraction pattern, shown in Fig. 7(b), which suggests

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that the cover has a fine mosaic structure. Indexing the spots in this pattern could not be related to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: any metal oxide in the system, further supporting the metallic nature of the covers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Radiation Damage Effects

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The high density of pits produced on the implanted side of the sample shown in Fig. 5(a) was confirmed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to be a consequence of radiation damage: Anodic polarization of a similar sample half-implanted with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 50 keV

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ions (which have a mass similar to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: produced the attack shown in Fig. 8. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: difference in density of small pit features is seen to be similar in Figs. 5(a) and 8, while "lacy" large pits

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also occur on both sides of the krypton-implanted sample. The implanted krypton thus causes radiation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: damage to the alloy substrate without the pit-moderating influence provided by molybdenum.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fig. 8. Optical micrograph of sample half-implanted with krypton and anodically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: polarized identically to the sample of Fig. 5(a).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In passing, it is worth observing that the passivating films formed on the 50 keV implanted samples

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (both molybdenum or krypton) would appear to inherit a high density of weak points, which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subsequently produce fine pits once the anodic potential is increased above the critical pitting potential.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This supports the "weak link" concept of the local breakdown of passive films (14).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: When alloy samples were implanted with 140 keV, instead of 50 keV, molybdenum ions the density of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pits on anodically polarized samples was much less. Figure 9(a) shows a region of one typical such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sample, showing some surface staining due to corrosion product. This sample, even though polarized

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for 15 minutes after breakdown, showed very few regions like this with pits of any kind. This is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consistent with the fact that radiation damage is reduced as the energy of the implanted ion is increased,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as has been observed by Howe et al (15) for the thermal oxidation of iron, and by Ashworth et al.(16)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for the growth of native oxides on iron. But while the density of pits is greatly reduced by using the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: higher implantation energy, the morphology of the pits is similar. Figure 10 shows an optical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: micrograph of one such pit on a sample which was only rinsed after anodic treatment by dipping into

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distilled water with no agitation, and dried in air. This procedure appears to avoid tearing the pit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: covers. Figure 10 suggests that the covers have relaxed following removal from solution, since they have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a slightly crinkled appearance, which is exaggerated by the Nomarski interference contrast technique

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (17), and which if viewed in the scanning electron microscope would appear like the pits in Fig. 6(a).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: DISCUSSION

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Despite the fact that the layer of implanted molybdenum is very thin, it does seem to be sufficient,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: particularly when implantation is carried out at the higher energy (140 keV) and an ion dose in excess

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: , to markedly improve the density of pitting attack on UNS S30100 stainless steel.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Comparison of Fig. 9(a) with the pits in Fig. 9(b), representing a similarly-treated unimplanted sample,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: clearly shows this, and also indicates that the pit growth rates are reduced considerably by molybdenum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: implantation of sufficient dose and energy.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Of additional interest in the observations of this study is the particular morphology of the pits produced

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in implanted material. Comparison of Figs. 5(b) and 6 demonstrates the differences in pit morphology

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: after anodic treatment of unimplanted and implanted material. The unimplanted alloy exhibits "lacy"

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: edges to the pits, while the implanted alloy pits are circular in plan view and have smooth covers, which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: include alloy metal, and little more than a small hole at their centre. It is assumed that the tears and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: folds seen at some of the covers are artifacts produced during processing of the sample.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We can suppose that the process of forming the "lacy" pits follows the scheme outlined in Fig. 11.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: After initial breakdown of the protective passive film by agglomeration of aggressive (chloride) ions (a)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a pit develops into the unprotected alloy below (b). The next stage is described by Pickering(18)(19),

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: using the concept of IR drop within the pit mouth, which leads to an active potential which can permit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dissolution of the vertical walls, leading to undercutting (c). The final stage involves the dissolution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Corrosion of Mo-implanted stainless steel

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fig. 11. Schematic development of "lacy" pits by undercutting mechanism.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the underside of the undercut alloy, resulting in a new perforation, which when it has occurred at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: many locations around the pit, results in the lacy effect (d). This model is similar to one proposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: recently by Egert (20) for surfaces with protective metallic coatings.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Howcver, the process of pit development in the molybdenum-implanted matcrial will be different due

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the highly alloyed surface layer. Consequently, if a pit forms undercutting can still occur but the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: breakthrough from below is impeded by the highly-protective alloy laycr. That there is an attempt at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: attack on the underside of the covers by thc highly corrosive pit solution is shown in Fig. 12. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pock-marks on the curled underside are clcarly scen, but no perforation is possible due to the highly-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloyed material. This model explains the metallic nature of the covers, as concluded from the detailed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: electron microscopic analysis.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fig. 12. Optical micrograph of curled-up covers from pits on a sample similar to that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shown in Figs. 5(a) and 9(a).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It follows that one rcason for the slow growth rate of the covered pits is that the growth is controlled

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by mass transport through the central perforation, rather than being due to the increasingly aggressive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: solution including, for example, a decreased pH, within the extremely "occluded" cell. Dissolution of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the highly concentratcd molybdenum might also contribute to inhibition of the anodic dissolutíon within

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the occluded pit. The crinkling effect (Fig. 10) could also be an indication of the relaxation occurring

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: after clastic stretching of the covers by the corrosion product build-up within the constricted pit.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CONCLUSIONS

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It is concluded that implanting molybdenum into an austenitic stainless stecl, at sufficient energy to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: avoid significant radiation damage and at doses sufficicnt to produce a ncar-surface maximum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: concentration of greater than 10 at%, can significantly reduce the pitting corrosion susceptibility under

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: anodic polarization control in marine-like environments. The feasibility of such processing for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: commercial purposes is, however, not proven.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: M. B. IVES et al.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The morphology of pits produced in molybdenum surface-implanted stainless steels is very different to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that produced on untreated commercial alloys. Pits are less dense, and those that do form are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constrained in their growth by the presence of a persistent cover of implanted alloy, and, perhaps, by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an inhibiting excess of molybdenum ions within the pit.
